source_text: Post hoc dicimus: sanctificetur nomen tuum, non quod optemus Deo ut sanctificetur orationibus nostris, sed quod petamus mus a Domino ut nomen eius sanctificetur in nobis. ceterum a quo Deus sanctificatur qui ipse sanctificat? sed quia ipse dixit:: sancti estote, quoniam et ego sanctus sum, id petimus et rogamus, ut qui in baptismo sanctificati sumus in eo quod esse coepimus perseueremus. et hoc cottidie deprecamur. opus est enim nobis cottidiana sanctificatio, ut qui cottidie delinquimus delicta nostra sanctificatione adsidua repurgemus. quae autem sit sanctificatio quae nobis de Dei dignatione confertur apostolus praedicat dicens: neque fornicarii neque idolis seruientes neque adulteri neque molles neque masculorum adpetitores neque fures neque fraudulenti neque ebriosi neque maledici neque raptores regnum Dei consequentur. et haec quidem fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed iustificati estis, sed sanctificati estis in nomine Domini Iesu Christi et in spiritu Dei nostri. sanctificatos nos dicit in nomine Domini Iesu Christi et in spiritu Dei nostri. haec sanctificatio ut in nobis permaneat oramus, et quia Dominus et iudex noster sanato a se et uiuificato comminatur iam non delinquere, ne quid ei deterius fiat, hanc continuis orationibus precem facimus, hoc diebus ac noctibus postulamus ut sanctificatio et uiuificatio quae de Dei gratia sumitur ipsius protectione seruetur.
thought_title: Hallowed be your name: daily sanctification
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the first petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'hallowed be your name,' after having discussed the opening address 'our Father.'
pass_a_gloss: After this we say: hallowed be your name, not that we wish for God that he be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask from the Lord that his name be hallowed in us. But by whom is God hallowed, who himself hallows? But because he himself said: be holy, since I also am holy, we seek and ask this, that we who have been hallowed in baptism may persevere in that which we have begun to be. And this we pray daily. For we need daily hallowing, so that we who sin daily may cleanse our sins by constant hallowing. What the hallowing is which is conferred on us by God's gracious favor the apostle proclaims, saying: neither fornicators nor idol-servers nor adulterers nor soft men nor pursuers of males nor thieves nor deceivers nor drunkards nor revilers nor robbers will obtain the kingdom of God. And these things indeed you were, but you were washed, but you were justified, but you were hallowed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God. He says we have been hallowed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God. We pray that this hallowing may remain in us, and because our Lord and judge threatens the man healed and made alive by him not to sin any more, lest something worse happen to him, we make this prayer with continual prayers, we ask this by days and nights, that the hallowing and making alive which is taken from God's grace may be preserved by his own protection.

choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering for the petition, preserving the passive subjunctive force of the Latin.
rejected: may your name be kept holy
let your name be made holy

choices.why: Keeps the verbal noun close to the petition's verb 'hallowed,' preserving the connection Cyprian draws between the petition and the ongoing process.
Renders the Latin term literally, preserving the ancient category without modernizing or softening it.
Literal rendering of the Latin phrase, keeping the active pursuit sense of 'adpetitores.'
Literal rendering of the noun, preserving the parallel with 'hallowing' and the active sense of God's work.
Renders the sense of God's condescending favor, which is the force of 'dignatio' here.

pass_b_english: After this we say: hallowed be your name. We do not mean that we wish God to be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask the Lord that his name may be hallowed in us. Besides, by whom is God hallowed, since he himself hallows? But because he himself said: "Be holy, for I too am holy" (Leviticus 11:44), we ask and beg this: that we who were hallowed in baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be. And we pray for this daily. For we need a daily hallowing, so that we who sin daily may cleanse our sins by constant hallowing. What this hallowing is that is conferred on us by God's gracious favor, the apostle proclaims when he says: "Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor soft men, nor pursuers of males, nor thieves, nor swindlers, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor robbers will obtain the kingdom of God. And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were justified, but you were hallowed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:9-11). He says that we are hallowed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. We pray that this hallowing may remain in us, and because our Lord and judge warns the man he has healed and made alive not to sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to him, we make this prayer with unceasing petitions. Day and night we ask this: that the hallowing and making alive that is received from God's grace may be preserved by his protection.

problems.why: "Fraudulenti" means swindlers/cheaters, not the greedy generally; wrong semantic range.

fixed: Changed 'the greedy' to 'swindlers' because the source 'fraudulenti' means cheaters/swindlers, not the greedy generally.

last_rejected.why: "Molles" means effeminate/passive homosexual partners, not generically "soft men."
last_rejected.fix: men who submit to homosexual acts
last_rejected.ruling: 'Molles' literally means 'soft'; 'soft men' is a valid literal rendering, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.why: "Adpetitores" means those who desire/seek; this is the active homosexual partner, not "pursuers."
last_rejected.ruling: 'Adpetitores' = pursuers/seekers; 'pursuers of males' accurately renders the Latin, not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: "Fraudulenti" means greedy/covetous persons (1 Cor 6:10 Vetus Latina), not "swindlers" who deceive others.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Fraudulenti' covers deceit/fraud; 'swindlers' is within normal range, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.why: "Maledici" means slanderers/revilers, those who speak evil; "abusive" is too weak and modern-ambiguous.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Maledici' = abusive/slanderous; 'the abusive' is within normal range, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.why: "Raptores" means kidnappers/slave-stealers (1 Cor 6:10), not "robbers" who take property by force.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Raptores' can mean robbers/plunderers; 'robbers' is within normal range, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.quote: the man he has healed and made alive
last_rejected.why: Greek/Latin "sanato" refers to the paralytic at Bethesda (John 5:14), not generic "healed"; "made alive" misses resurrection connotation.
last_rejected.fix: the one he has made whole and given life to
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sanato' = healed; 'made alive' renders 'uiuificato'. Both are accurate; specific reference is implicit, not lost.

last_rejected.quote: the apostle proclaims when he says
last_rejected.why: Voice marker "apostolus praedicat" identifies Paul per work brief; English "apostle" without name obscures this.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Apostolus' = 'the apostle'; rendering it as such is accurate. Adding 'Paul' would be interpretation, not correction.

last_rejected.quote: And such were some of you.
last_rejected.why: Cyprian's text says you were these things; 'some' is not in the Latin and weakens the claim.
last_rejected.ruling: "haec quidem fuistis" (you were these things); "such were some of you" is the standard rendering of 1 Cor 6:11 (KJV/ESV 'such were some of you'). It's within range, not a change of meaning.
